summary: Lists the numbers assigned for networks, protocols and similar identifiers used in the early Internet. Such lists were reissued as assignments changed. This RFC is historic. Replaced by RFC 776.

eli5.summary: Like a phone book for the early internet, this list says which number belongs to which network or service. A newer edition replaced it.

subtitle: A registry of network and protocol identifiers assigned in the early Internet.

tldr.problem: The early Internet needed standard numbers for networks, protocols, ports and other identifiers, but there was no single place to look them up.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC publishes the assigned numbers: network numbers 0-38, protocol versions, protocol types, port numbers, and link numbers, managed centrally by Jon Postel.
tldr.outcome: Applications could use a standard reference for identifiers. Historic; replaced by RFC 776.

today: RFC 770 is Historic. RFC 776 replaced it with updated assignments as the Internet grew.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: This RFC documents the assigned numbers used in network protocols of the early 1980s Internet. It lists networks, protocols, ports and other identifiers in one place, managed by Jon Postel at USC Information Sciences Institute. When someone needed to develop a new protocol or application, they would contact Postel to receive a unique number assignment.
sections.eli5: This book lists all the numbers used in early Internet systems and who owns which one.

sections.title: Networks and Protocols
sections.content: The RFC assigns network numbers (0-38, an 8-bit field) to the interconnected networks of the time: ARPANET, satellite networks, packet radio systems, and academic networks like MIT's CHAOS network and Xerox Ethernet. It also lists 15 Internet Protocol versions and protocol identifiers 0-79 for the next-layer protocol field in IP headers: protocols like TCP (6), UDP (17), and experimental ones.
sections.eli5: Each network and each protocol type gets a unique number so computers know what they are talking to.

sections.title: Ports and Links
sections.content: The RFC specifies port numbers (or sockets in some systems) for services like Telnet (port 23), File Transfer (port 21), and SMTP mail (port 57). Well-known service ports use the low 8 bits of a larger field. The document also assigns link numbers for the ARPANET Host/IMP interface, a 12-bit message-ID field with the high 8 bits as 'link' and the low 4 bits for protocol-specific use.
sections.eli5: Each service on a computer listens on its own numbered mailbox, so messages get to the right program.
